title: Sunset without objects
hookLine: Agastya teaches Rama a hymn to the sun mid-battle; worship needs no objects
carry: the sun is the god you can see
last: FAMILY ARTI — A HOUSEHOLDER'S HOME IS HOLY GROUND.

lines: A BATTLEFIELD. NO TEMPLE, NO LAMP.
SOMETHING YOU CAN DO RIGHT HERE.
cards: The war in Lanka has gone on and on. Rama stands facing Ravana, and for once he's worn out, wondering how this fight can be won. There's no temple here.
No lamp, no bell, no flowers. Just dust, arrows, and the sun overhead. Then an old sage makes his way across the battlefield to him: Agastya.
Rama, he says, listen. I'll teach you something you can do right here, right now, with nothing in your hands.

teach.h: AGASTYA'S HYMN: THE HEART OF THE SUN.
teach.b: In the Ramayana, what Agastya teaches is a hymn to the sun, the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun.
It praises the sun as the light in all the gods, Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and more, and as the witness of everything people do.
Rama looks toward the sun, recites the hymn, sips water three times to purify himself, and turns back to the fight with fresh strength. Soon after, Ravana falls. Here's the teaching.

teach.h: THE GOD YOU CAN ACTUALLY SEE.
teach.b: In Hindu tradition the sun is often called the god you can actually see. You don't need an image or a shelf to find him; he's in front of you every day, rising and setting.
That's why so many Hindus pour water toward the sun at dawn, as you did on day one hundred fifteen, and why worship never depends on having the right objects.

teach.h: THE LAMP: A LITTLE SUN INDOORS.
teach.b: One way to see this week's arti lamp: every evening, as the sun goes down, a household lights a small flame and holds it up, a little sun carried indoors for the night.
That's a reading, not a rule, but it means this: when you have nothing, you still have the original flame.

Anywhere, you can turn west at dusk, put your hands together, and watch the light finish its path. One practical thing: never stare straight into the sun. Watch the sky around it, the colors, the edges of the clouds.

how: Many Hindus honor the sun directly, pouring water toward it at dawn or bowing to it at the twilight junctions, and some recite the Aditya Hridayam; when no shrine is available, some simply face the rising or setting sun with folded hands.

s: Rama prayed to the sun right on the battlefield
Agastya taught him a hymn to the sun, and Rama recited it, facing the sun, before fighting on.
Hindu worship is impossible without a lamp and a shrine
the sun is the god you can see: face it with folded hands.
the practice asks you to stare into the sun
never stare straight into it; watch the sky around it.

games.q: it's evening and you're in a hotel room with no lamp, no shrine, nothing. what's Rama's battlefield answer?
o: face the setting sun, hands together, and pray.
buy a lamp before you do anything.
games.why: Rama had nothing but the sun, and it was enough. the sun is the god you can see; the arti lamp is a small stand-in for it.

practice: If you can, turn toward the west, toward a window or where the sun sets even if it's hidden right now; if it's not evening, picture the last sunset you remember well.
Put your hands together at your chest if you'd like, and look at the sky around the sun, never at the sun itself.
Let the color be the flame and the whole horizon the plate: nothing to hold, nothing to light, just the original flame and you in front of it.

wordCard.voice: Surya, the sun, honored as the god you can see: Rama prayed to him on a battlefield, and you can face him at dusk with nothing in your hands. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit sūrya: the sun, honored as a deity in the Vedas and at the daily junctions.
